extracted.intended_audience: journalism researchers, editors, journalists, and media studies students
extracted.subtask_description: A taxonomy for assessing the news value or newsworthiness of stories, updating classical news values to reflect digital-era factors (e.g., social media, audio-visuals). Useful for editors deciding what to publish or researchers analyzing news selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories generated by, or available first to, the news organization (interviews, letters, surveys, photos, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers material that the outlet uniquely possesses or can claim first publication of (e.g., exclusive interviews, original photos, proprietary surveys). Exclusive access increases newsworthiness because it cannot be immediately reproduced by competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad news
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with particularly negative overtones such as death, injury, defeat, and loss (of jobs, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative outcomes and harms are inherently newsworthy; items featuring loss, tragedy, or failure are prioritized due to their salience and audience interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning conflict such as controversies, arguments, splits, strikes, fights, insurrections, and warfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any form of disagreement, contestation or opposing forces (political, social, legal, military, industrial disputes) increases attention and perceived importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with an element of surprise, contrast, and/or the unusual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unusual events, unexpected outcomes, or striking contrasts make stories stand out and attract interest; novelty matters even if otherwise minor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audio-visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with arresting photographs, video, audio, and/or which can be illustrated with infographics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visually or sonically rich material gains prominence in digital/news environments because it is more engaging and more easily repurposed across platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shareability
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that are likely to generate sharing and comments via Facebook, Twitter, and other forms of social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictable social-media traction (emotionally charged, easily summarized, listicles, 'clickable' formats) raises a story's value to publishers focused on engagement metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Soft stories concerning sex, showbusiness, sport, lighter human interest, animals, or offering opportunities for humorous treatment, witty headlines, or lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Light, amusing, or celebrity-oriented content is newsworthy for its audience-appeal and potential for entertaining presentation formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning an unfolding drama such as escapes, accidents, searches, sieges, rescues, battles, or court cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ongoing, unfolding situations with suspense and narrative tension attract sustained coverage because they invite continued audience attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about subjects already in the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity matters: developments, updates, or consequences of previously reported stories are prioritized because audiences expect ongoing coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: The power elite
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning powerful individuals, organisations, institutions, or corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events or actions involving political, economic, or cultural elites are newsworthy due to their influence and perceived significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about groups or nations perceived to be influential with, or culturally or historically familiar to, the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geographic, cultural, or historical proximity to the audience raises story value; perceived audience interest shapes selection (familiarity and influence matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories perceived as sufficiently significant either in the numbers of people involved or in potential impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale and potential consequences (large numbers affected, major impacts) increase a story's priority for coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning people who are already famous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fame itself confers newsworthiness: events involving well-known individuals attract audience attention regardless of other characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good news
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with positive overtones such as recoveries, breakthroughs, cures, wins, and celebrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive developments are valued for balance and audience uplift; breakthroughs and successes are singled out as newsworthy in their own right.

rubrics_metrics.name: News organization's agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that set or fit the news organization's own agenda, whether ideological, commercial, or part of a specific campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial priorities, campaigns, ideological positions, or commercial strategies can make certain stories more likely to be pursued and foregrounded.
